claim: Drosophila Nab2 is orthologous to a human protein lost in a form of inherited intellectual disability.
source: The Drosophila polyadenosine RNA binding protein Nab2, which is orthologous to a human protein lost in a form of inherited intellectual disability, controls adult locomotion, axon projection, dendritic arborization, and memory through a largely undefined set of target RNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work establishing the orthology and disease association.

claim: Drosophila Nab2 controls adult locomotion, axon projection, dendritic arborization, and memory.
source: The Drosophila polyadenosine RNA binding protein Nab2, which is orthologous to a human protein lost in a form of inherited intellectual disability, controls adult locomotion, axon projection, dendritic arborization, and memory through a largely undefined set of target RNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and is presented as established knowledge.

claim: Nab2 regulates splicing of approximately 150 exons/introns in the head transcriptome.
source: Here, we show a specific role for Nab2 in regulating splicing of ~150 exons/introns in the head transcriptome and focus on retention of a male-specific exon in the sex determination factor Sex-lethal (Sxl) that is enriched in female neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nab2 regulates retention of a male-specific exon in Sex-lethal (Sxl) that is enriched in female neurons.
source: Here, we show a specific role for Nab2 in regulating splicing of ~150 exons/introns in the head transcriptome and focus on retention of a male-specific exon in the sex determination factor Sex-lethal (Sxl) that is enriched in female neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and RT-PCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sxl splicing is regulated in females by N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification by the Mettl3 complex.
source: Previous studies have revealed that this splicing event is regulated in females by N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification by the Mettl3 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Nab2 associates with Sxl pre-mRNA in neurons.
source: At a molecular level, Nab2 associates with Sxl pre-mRNA in neurons and limits Sxl m6A methylation at specific sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nab2 limits Sxl m6A methylation at specific sites.
source: At a molecular level, Nab2 associates with Sxl pre-mRNA in neurons and limits Sxl m6A methylation at specific sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP and DART-Sanger sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reducing expression of Mettl3 rescues mutant phenotypes in Nab2 flies.
source: In parallel, reducing expression of the Mettl3, Mettl3 complex components, or the m6A reader Ythdc1 rescues mutant phenotypes in Nab2 flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reducing expression of Mettl3 complex components rescues mutant phenotypes in Nab2 flies.
source: In parallel, reducing expression of the Mettl3, Mettl3 complex components, or the m6A reader Ythdc1 rescues mutant phenotypes in Nab2 flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reducing expression of the m6A reader Ythdc1 rescues mutant phenotypes in Nab2 flies.
source: In parallel, reducing expression of the Mettl3, Mettl3 complex components, or the m6A reader Ythdc1 rescues mutant phenotypes in Nab2 flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nab2 is an inhibitor of m6A methylation.
source: Overall, these data identify Nab2 as an inhibitor of m6A methylation and imply significant overlap between Nab2 and Mettl3 regulated RNAs in neuronal tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP and DART-Sanger sequencing data showing increased m6A in Nab2 mutants.

claim: There is significant overlap between Nab2 and Mettl3 regulated RNAs in neuronal tissue.
source: Overall, these data identify Nab2 as an inhibitor of m6A methylation and imply significant overlap between Nab2 and Mettl3 regulated RNAs in neuronal tissue.
evidence: This claim is inferred from genetic interactions and splicing data.

claim: There are approximately 1500 RBPs that distribute between the nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: There are an estimated ~1500 RBPs that distribute between the nucleus and cytoplasm (Gerstberger et al., 2014), and each has the potential to interact with RNAs to modulate post-transcriptional gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gerstberger et al., 2014.

claim: RBPs play critical roles in neurons.
source: The critical roles of RBPs in neurons are highlighted by many studies that reveal the importance of this class of proteins in brain development and function (Darnell and Richter, 2012) and by the prevalence of human neurological diseases linked to mutations in genes encoding RBPs (Brinegar and Cooper, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Human neurological diseases are linked to mutations in genes encoding RBPs.
source: The critical roles of RBPs in neurons are highlighted by many studies that reveal the importance of this class of proteins in brain development and function (Darnell and Richter, 2012) and by the prevalence of human neurological diseases linked to mutations in genes encoding RBPs (Brinegar and Cooper, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brinegar and Cooper, 2016.

claim: ZC3H14 binds with high affinity to poly(A) RNAs via a set of C-terminal tandem Cys-Cys-Cys-His type ZnF domains.
source: Among these is the zinc finger Cys-Cys-Cys-His-type containing 14 (ZC3H14) protein, which binds with high affinity to poly(A) RNAs via a set of C-terminal tandem Cys-Cys-Cys-His type ZnF domains (Leung et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leung et al., 2009.

claim: Mutations in the human ZC3H14 gene are associated with a heritable form of intellectual disability.
source: ZC3H14 is broadly expressed in many tissues and cell types but mutations in the human ZC3H14 gene are associated with a heritable form of intellectual disability (Pak et al., 2011), implying an important requirement for this protein in the central nervous system.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pak et al., 2011.

claim: Zygotic loss of ZC3H14 in mice and Drosophila impairs neuronal function.
source: Zygotic loss of ZC3H14 in mice and Drosophila impairs neuronal function (Pak et al., 2011; Roxas et al., 2017), while neuron-specific depletion of Drosophila Nab2 is sufficient to replicate these effects (Pak et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pak et al., 2011 and Roxas et al., 2017.

claim: Neuron-specific depletion of Drosophila Nab2 is sufficient to impair neuronal function.
source: Zygotic loss of ZC3H14 in mice and Drosophila impairs neuronal function (Pak et al., 2011; Roxas et al., 2017), while neuron-specific depletion of Drosophila Nab2 is sufficient to replicate these effects (Pak et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pak et al., 2011.

claim: Expression of human ZC3H14 in Nab2-deficient neurons rescues neuronal defects.
source: Reciprocally, expression of human ZC3H14 in Nab2-deficient neurons rescues this defect, demonstrating a high degree of functional conservation between human ZC3H14 and Drosophila Nab2 (Kelly et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kelly et al., 2014.

claim: There is a high degree of functional conservation between human ZC3H14 and Drosophila Nab2.
source: Reciprocally, expression of human ZC3H14 in Nab2-deficient neurons rescues this defect, demonstrating a high degree of functional conservation between human ZC3H14 and Drosophila Nab2 (Kelly et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kelly et al., 2014 and rescue experiments.

claim: Neuronal ZC3H14/Nab2 can be divided into a nuclear pool and a small cytoplasmic pool.
source: Neuronal ZC3H14/Nab2 can be divided into two pools: a nuclear pool that accounts for the majority of ZC3H14/Nab2 in the cell, and a small cytoplasmic pool of protein detected in mRNA ribonucleoprotein particles (mRNPs) of axons and dendrites (Leung et al., 2009; Roxas et al., 2017; Bienkowski et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Leung et al., 2009; Roxas et al., 2017; Bienkowski et al., 2017.

claim: Depletion of Nab2 in Drosophila neurons causes defects in axon projection within the brain mushroom bodies.
source: Depletion of both pools in Drosophila neurons causes defects in axon projection within the brain mushroom bodies (MBs) (Kelly et al., 2016), a pair of neuropil structures involved in olfactory learning and memory (Armstrong et al., 1998; Heisenberg, 2003), and excess branching of dendrites on peripheral sensory neurons (Corgiat et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kelly et al., 2016.

claim: Depletion of Nab2 in Drosophila neurons causes excess branching of dendrites on peripheral sensory neurons.
source: Depletion of both pools in Drosophila neurons causes defects in axon projection within the brain mushroom bodies (MBs) (Kelly et al., 2016), a pair of neuropil structures involved in olfactory learning and memory (Armstrong et al., 1998; Heisenberg, 2003), and excess branching of dendrites on peripheral sensory neurons (Corgiat et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Corgiat et al., 2022.

claim: Nab2 physically associates with the Drosophila Fragile-X mental retardation protein homolog in the neuronal cytoplasm.
source: The Nab2 requirement in MBs is linked to a physical association between Nab2 and the Drosophila Fragile-X mental retardation protein homolog (Wan et al., 2000) in the neuronal cytoplasm and translational repression of shared Nab2-Fmr1 target RNAs (Bienkowski et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wan et al., 2000 and Bienkowski et al., 2017.

claim: Nab2 and Fmr1 translationally repress shared target RNAs.
source: The Nab2 requirement in MBs is linked to a physical association between Nab2 and the Drosophila Fragile-X mental retardation protein homolog (Wan et al., 2000) in the neuronal cytoplasm and translational repression of shared Nab2-Fmr1 target RNAs (Bienkowski et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bienkowski et al., 2017.

claim: Nab2 limits dendritic branching through effects on the cytoplasmic planar cell polarity pathway.
source: Genetic data indicate that Nab2 limits dendritic branching through effects on the cytoplasmic planar cell polarity pathway (Corgiat et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Corgiat et al., 2022.

claim: RNA sequencing reads across the Nab2 gene are almost completely eliminated in Nab2ex3 mutants.
source: RNA sequencing reads across the Nab2 gene are almost completely eliminated in Nab2ex3 mutants, confirming the genetic background and integrity of this analysis pipeline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Principal component analysis confirms that the 12 RNA-seq datasets distribute into four clusters that diverge significantly based on genotype and sex.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) performed with DESeq2 output data confirms that the 12 RNA-seq datasets distribute into four clusters that diverge significantly from one another based on genotype (Nab2ex3 vs. Nab2pex41 control; PC1 58% variance) and sex (male vs. female; PC2 26% variance) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DESeq2 analysis detects 3799 genes in females that exhibit statistically significant differences in RNA abundance between Nab2ex3 and control.
source: The DESeq2 analysis detects 3799 and 1545 genes in females and males, respectively, that exhibit statistically significant differences in RNA abundance between Nab2ex3 and control (BH-adjusted p-value/false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by DESeq2 analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: DESeq2 analysis detects 1545 genes in males that exhibit statistically significant differences in RNA abundance between Nab2ex3 and control.
source: The DESeq2 analysis detects 3799 and 1545 genes in females and males, respectively, that exhibit statistically significant differences in RNA abundance between Nab2ex3 and control (BH-adjusted p-value/false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by DESeq2 analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: There is a high degree of correlation (R = 0.79) in fold-changes of significantly different RNAs between female and male samples.
source: Comparison of fold-changes (Nab2ex3 vs. control) among these significantly different RNAs reveals a high degree of correlation in female vs. male samples (R = 0.79), particularly among RNAs whose levels are most elevated upon Nab2 loss (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Applying a twofold change cutoff yields 453 significantly changed RNAs in females (294 'up,' 159 'down').
source: Applying a twofold change cutoff (|log2[fold-change]| ≥ 1) trims these sets to 453 significantly changed RNAs in females (294 'up,' 159 'down') and 305 significantly changed RNAs in males (150 'up,' 155 'down') (Figure 1C), which merge into a combined set of 570 significantly affected RNAs that trend similarly in heatmap analysis of mutant vs. control samples (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by DESeq2 analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Applying a twofold change cutoff yields 305 significantly changed RNAs in males (150 'up,' 155 'down').
source: Applying a twofold change cutoff (|log2[fold-change]| ≥ 1) trims these sets to 453 significantly changed RNAs in females (294 'up,' 159 'down') and 305 significantly changed RNAs in males (150 'up,' 155 'down') (Figure 1C), which merge into a combined set of 570 significantly affected RNAs that trend similarly in heatmap analysis of mutant vs. control samples (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by DESeq2 analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A majority of the 453 affected 'female' RNAs are mRNAs (439).
source: A majority of the 453 affected 'female' RNAs are mRNAs (439) and the remaining are snoRNAs (8), snRNAs (1), pre-rRNAs (1), and tRNAs (4) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA classification shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The number of significantly changed RNAs in Nab2ex3 female and male heads represents a small fraction of RNAs detected in heads (2.2 and 3.7% in males and females, respectively).
source: Overall, the number of significantly changed RNAs (|log2[fold-change]| ≥ 1 and FDR < 0.05) in Nab2ex3 female and male heads represents a small fraction of RNAs detected in heads (2.2 and 3.7% in males and females, respectively), suggesting that Nab2 normally contributes to RNA-specific regulatory mechanisms in Drosophila head tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by calculation from RNA-seq data.

claim: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis detects significant enrichment for 'RNA splicing' GO term within the upregulated group of RNAs in both sexes.
source: This filtering uncovers significant enrichment (p<0.05) for 'RNA splicing' GO (GO:0008380) within the upregulated group of RNAs in both sexes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In Nab2ex3 females, 32 of 155 genes annotated under the 'RNA splicing' term are present among upregulated RNAs.
source: In Nab2ex3 females, 32 of 155 genes annotated under this term are present among upregulated RNAs; whereas in males, 75 of 159 genes annotated under this term are present among upregulated RNAs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In Nab2ex3 males, 75 of 159 genes annotated under the 'RNA splicing' term are present among upregulated RNAs.
source: In Nab2ex3 females, 32 of 155 genes annotated under this term are present among upregulated RNAs; whereas in males, 75 of 159 genes annotated under this term are present among upregulated RNAs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: DEXSeq analysis detects 151 affected RNAs in Nab2ex3 females.
source: To test whether Nab2 loss results in unannotated or aberrant splicing events among head RNAs, DEXSeq analysis (Anders et al., 2012) was performed to scan for differential abundance of individual exons relative to other exons within the same transcript. This analysis detects 151 affected RNAs in Nab2ex3 females and 114 in Nab2ex3 males (Table 1), with many top-ranked transcripts encoding factors with roles in behavior, neurodevelopment, and/or neural function (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by DEXSeq analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: DEXSeq analysis detects 114 affected RNAs in Nab2ex3 males.
source: To test whether Nab2 loss results in unannotated or aberrant splicing events among head RNAs, DEXSeq analysis (Anders et al., 2012) was performed to scan for differential abundance of individual exons relative to other exons within the same transcript. This analysis detects 151 affected RNAs in Nab2ex3 females and 114 in Nab2ex3 males (Table 1), with many top-ranked transcripts encoding factors with roles in behavior, neurodevelopment, and/or neural function (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by DEXSeq analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The most statistically significant exon usage change in either sex is female-specific inclusion of exon 3 in the Sex lethal (Sxl) mRNA (p=3.08 × 10–235).
source: Among the 151 most affected RNAs, the most statistically significant exon usage change in either sex is female-specific inclusion of exon 3 in the Sex lethal (Sxl) mRNA (p=3.08 × 10–235).
evidence: This claim is supported by DEXSeq analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Visualizing Sxl RNA-Seq reads with IGV confirms a large increase in exon 3 reads in Nab2ex3 females relative to control females.
source: Visualizing Sxl RNA-Seq reads with Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) (Robinson et al., 2017) confirms a large increase in exon 3 reads in Nab2ex3 females (Nab2ex3 F) relative to control females (control F), and also reveals retention of ~500 bases of intron 3 sequence in Nab2ex3 females (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by IGV visualization shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IGV reveals retention of approximately 500 bases of intron 3 sequence in Nab2ex3 females.
source: Visualizing Sxl RNA-Seq reads with Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) (Robinson et al., 2017) confirms a large increase in exon 3 reads in Nab2ex3 females (Nab2ex3 F) relative to control females (control F), and also reveals retention of ~500 bases of intron 3 sequence in Nab2ex3 females (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by IGV visualization shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Quantification of reads across the entire Sxl locus detects an approximately 1.5-fold increase in the overall abundance of the Sxl mRNA in Nab2ex3 females compared to control females.
source: Quantification of reads across the entire Sxl locus detects an ~1.5-fold increase in the overall abundance of the Sxl mRNA in Nab2ex3 females compared to control females.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of RNA-seq reads.

claim: RT-PCR confirms the presence of the mis-spliced exon 2-exon 3-exon 4 mRNA transcript in Nab2ex3 females.
source: Parallel reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) on fly heads using Sxl primers that detect exon 2-exon 4 (control females) and exon 2-exon 3-exon 4 (control males) confirms the presence of the mis-spliced exon 2-exon 3-exon 4 mRNA transcript in Nab2ex3 females (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RT-PCR reveals an approximately 1 kb band in Nab2ex3 females that is aberrantly spliced transcript incorporating 503 bases of intron 3.
source: RT-PCR also reveals an ~1 kb band in Nab2ex3 females (arrowhead, Figure 3B) that sequencing identifies as aberrantly spliced transcript that incorporates 503 bases of intron 3 leading up to a cryptic 5′ splice site (i.e., exon 2-exon 3-intron 3503-exon 4), which matches the Sxl intron 3 sequencing reads observed in IGV (see Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: qRT-PCR confirms a statistically significant increase in the inclusion of the male-specific exon 3 in Nab2ex3 female heads.
source: qRT-PCR confirms a statistically significant increase in the inclusion of the male-specific exon 3 in females with a concomitant decrease in the level of correctly spliced (exon 2-exon 4) transcript in both Nab2ex3 and Mettl3null female heads (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: qRT-PCR confirms a concomitant decrease in the level of correctly spliced (exon 2-exon 4) Sxl transcript in Nab2ex3 female heads.
source: qRT-PCR confirms a statistically significant increase in the inclusion of the male-specific exon 3 in females with a concomitant decrease in the level of correctly spliced (exon 2-exon 4) transcript in both Nab2ex3 and Mettl3null female heads (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Immunoblotting analysis reveals reduced levels of Sxl protein in Nab2ex3 female heads compared to control.
source: Indeed, immunoblotting analysis reveals reduced levels of Sxl protein in Nab2ex3 female heads compared to control or Mettl3 null heads (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: RT-PCR analysis detects Sxl exon 3 retention in Nab2ex3 samples prepared from the thorax.
source: Significantly, RT-PCR analysis of Sxl mRNA in dissected control and Nab2ex3 females detects exon 3 retention in Nab2ex3 samples prepared from the thorax, but little to no retention in the abdomen and ovary (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: RT-PCR analysis detects little to no Sxl exon 3 retention in Nab2ex3 samples prepared from the abdomen and ovary.
source: Significantly, RT-PCR analysis of Sxl mRNA in dissected control and Nab2ex3 females detects exon 3 retention in Nab2ex3 samples prepared from the thorax, but little to no retention in the abdomen and ovary (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Nab2 is only necessary to direct Sxl exon 3 exclusion in specific tissues or cell types such as neurons.
source: This result implies that Nab2 is only necessary to direct Sxl exon 3 exclusion in specific tissues or cell types such as neurons, which are enriched in the head (brain) and thorax (ventral nerve cord).
evidence: This claim is inferred from tissue-specific RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Bioinformatic scan detected candidate Sxl binding sites as the single most abundant RBP motif within the Nab2-regulated MISO events in females.
source: This unbiased scan detected candidate Sxl binding sites as the single most abundant RBP motif within the Nab2-regulated MISO events in females (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RBP motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Sxl motifs were not detected as enriched in the male Nab2ex3 MISO dataset.
source: Notably, Sxl motifs were not detected as enriched in the male Nab2ex3 MISO dataset, which otherwise strongly resembles the remaining group of female-enriched RBP motifs (e.g., the hnRNPL homolog smooth [sm], RNA binding protein-9 [Rbp9], the U1-SNRNPA homolog sans fille [snf], and the U2-SNRNP component [U2AF50]).
evidence: This claim is supported by RBP motif enrichment analysis.

claim: The Sxl target transformer (tra) was not recovered in the Nab2ex3 MISO or DESeq2 datasets.
source: Intriguingly, the Sxl target transformer (tra) and the Tra target double-sex (dsx) (Sánchez et al., 2001; Horabin and Schedl, 1993) were not recovered in the Nab2ex3 MISO or DESeq2 datasets, and IGV reads show little evidence of altered structure of tra and dsx RNAs as compared to Nab2pex41 controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by MISO, DESeq2, and IGV analysis.

claim: The Tra target double-sex (dsx) was not recovered in the Nab2ex3 MISO or DESeq2 datasets.
source: Intriguingly, the Sxl target transformer (tra) and the Tra target double-sex (dsx) (Sánchez et al., 2001; Horabin and Schedl, 1993) were not recovered in the Nab2ex3 MISO or DESeq2 datasets, and IGV reads show little evidence of altered structure of tra and dsx RNAs as compared to Nab2pex41 controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by MISO, DESeq2, and IGV analysis.

claim: SxlM8 contains a 110 bp deletion spanning the 3′-end of intron 2 and 5′-end of exon 3.
source: SxlM8 contains a 110 bp deletion spanning the 3′-end of intron 2 and 5′-end of exon 3, and consequently undergoes constitutive splicing to the feminized exon 2-exon 4 variant regardless of sex (Figure 4A, top panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and schematic in Figure 4A.

claim: SxlM8 undergoes constitutive splicing to the feminized exon 2-exon 4 variant regardless of sex.
source: SxlM8 contains a 110 bp deletion spanning the 3′-end of intron 2 and 5′-end of exon 3, and consequently undergoes constitutive splicing to the feminized exon 2-exon 4 variant regardless of sex (Figure 4A, top panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and schematic in Figure 4A.

claim: The SxlM8 allele is male-lethal in both control and Nab2ex3 backgrounds.
source: Consistent with the original report describing SxlM8 (Barbash and Cline, 1995), the allele is male-lethal in both control and Nab2ex3 backgrounds.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic data and citation to Barbash and Cline, 1995.

claim: Heterozygosity for SxlM8 produces strong rescue of Nab2ex3 mutant female viability from approximately 4% to 71%.
source: However, heterozygosity for SxlM8 produces strong rescue of Nab2ex3 mutant female viability from ~4% to 71% (SxlM8/+;;Nab2ex3) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SxlM8/+;;Nab2ex3 females show improved locomotion in a negative geotaxis assay relative to Nab2ex3 females.
source: SxlM8/+;;Nab2ex3 females also show improved locomotion in a negative geotaxis assay (Figure 4B) and lengthened lifespan (Figure 4C) relative to Nab2ex3 females.
evidence: This claim is supported by negative geotaxis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: SxlM8/+;;Nab2ex3 females show lengthened lifespan relative to Nab2ex3 females.
source: SxlM8/+;;Nab2ex3 females also show improved locomotion in a negative geotaxis assay (Figure 4B) and lengthened lifespan (Figure 4C) relative to Nab2ex3 females.
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Female-specific rescue of Nab2ex3 by SxlM8 indicates that partial restoration of Sxl expression can compensate for Nab2 loss.
source: This female-specific rescue of Nab2ex3 by SxlM8 indicates that partial restoration of Sxl expression can compensate for Nab2 loss.
evidence: This claim is inferred from genetic rescue data.

claim: A single copy of msl-2kmA significantly rescues defects in viability in Nab2ex3 females.
source: A single copy of msl-2kmA significantly rescues defects in viability (Figure 4D), locomotion (Figure 4E), and lifespan (Figure 4F) in Nab2ex3 females.
evidence: This claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A single copy of msl-2kmA significantly rescues defects in locomotion in Nab2ex3 females.
source: A single copy of msl-2kmA significantly rescues defects in viability (Figure 4D), locomotion (Figure 4E), and lifespan (Figure 4F) in Nab2ex3 females.
evidence: This claim is supported by locomotion data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A single copy of msl-2kmA significantly rescues defects in lifespan in Nab2ex3 females.
source: A single copy of msl-2kmA significantly rescues defects in viability (Figure 4D), locomotion (Figure 4E), and lifespan (Figure 4F) in Nab2ex3 females.
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A second msl-2 mutant allele over a deficiency that uncovers the msl-2 locus (msl-l227/Exel7016) rescues Nab2ex3 mutant phenotypes.
source: Furthermore, a second msl-2 mutant allele over a deficiency that uncovers the msl-2 locus (msl-l227/Exel7016) (Zhou et al., 1995), as well as roX1 and mle loss-of-function alleles, rescue Nab2ex3 mutant phenotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: roX1 loss-of-function alleles rescue Nab2ex3 mutant phenotypes.
source: Furthermore, a second msl-2 mutant allele over a deficiency that uncovers the msl-2 locus (msl-l227/Exel7016) (Zhou et al., 1995), as well as roX1 and mle loss-of-function alleles, rescue Nab2ex3 mutant phenotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: mle loss-of-function alleles rescue Nab2ex3 mutant phenotypes.
source: Furthermore, a second msl-2 mutant allele over a deficiency that uncovers the msl-2 locus (msl-l227/Exel7016) (Zhou et al., 1995), as well as roX1 and mle loss-of-function alleles, rescue Nab2ex3 mutant phenotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rescue of Nab2ex3 females by msl-2, mle, and roX1 alleles provides evidence that the DCC pathway is inappropriately activated upon Nab2 loss.
source: Given that Msl-2 is not normally active in adult female tissues (Amrein and Axel, 1997; Meller et al., 1997) and its forced expression reduces female viability (Kelley et al., 1995), rescue of Nab2ex3 females by these msl-2, mle, and roX1 alleles provides evidence that the DCC pathway is inappropriately activated upon Nab2 loss.
evidence: This claim is inferred from genetic rescue data and citations to prior work.

claim: The Mettl3-containing methyltransferase complex promotes exon 3 exclusion in females by depositing m6A within Sxl exon 3 and flanking introns.
source: One mechanism that promotes exon 3 exclusion in females is based on N6-methylation of adenosines (m6A) in Sxl pre-mRNA by the Methyltransferase like-3 (Mettl3)-containing methyltransferase complex (Haussmann et al., 2016; Lence et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haussmann et al., 2016 and Lence et al., 2016.

claim: Inactivating mutations in components of the m6A 'writer' complex masculinize the pattern of exon 3 splicing in female flies in a manner similar to Nab2ex3.
source: Inactivating mutations in components of this m6A 'writer' complex masculinize the pattern of exon 3 splicing in female flies in a manner similar to Nab2ex3 and molecular studies indicate that the Mettl3 complex promotes exon 3 exclusion in females by depositing m6A within Sxl exon 3 and flanking introns (Haussmann et al., 2016; Lence et al., 2016; Kan et al., 2017; Kan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Homozygosity for the Mettl3null allele reduces adult viability.
source: Consistent with prior work (Haussmann et al., 2016; Lence et al., 2016; Kan et al., 2017), homozygosity for the Mettl3null allele reduces adult viability (Figure 5A), decreases locomotion in a negative geotaxis assay (Figure 5B), and shortens lifespan (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 5A and citations to prior work.

claim: Homozygosity for the Mettl3null allele decreases locomotion in a negative geotaxis assay.
source: Consistent with prior work (Haussmann et al., 2016; Lence et al., 2016; Kan et al., 2017), homozygosity for the Mettl3null allele reduces adult viability (Figure 5A), decreases locomotion in a negative geotaxis assay (Figure 5B), and shortens lifespan (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by locomotion data shown in Figure 5B and citations to prior work.

claim: Homozygosity for the Mettl3null allele shortens lifespan.
source: Consistent with prior work (Haussmann et al., 2016; Lence et al., 2016; Kan et al., 2017), homozygosity for the Mettl3null allele reduces adult viability (Figure 5A), decreases locomotion in a negative geotaxis assay (Figure 5B), and shortens lifespan (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5C and citations to prior work.

claim: Mettl3null heterozygosity suppresses viability defects in Nab2ex3 females.
source: However, Mettl3null heterozygosity has the inverse effect of suppressing each of these defects in Nab2ex3 females: Nab2ex3,Mettl3null/+ mutant females show approximately 3-fold higher viability (Figure 5A), 6-fold higher climbing rates (at the 30 s time point; Figure 5B), and 1.75-fold longer lifespan (Figure 5C) than Nab2ex3 mutant females.
evidence: This claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Nab2ex3,Mettl3null/+ mutant females show approximately 3-fold higher viability than Nab2ex3 mutant females.
source: However, Mettl3null heterozygosity has the inverse effect of suppressing each of these defects in Nab2ex3 females: Nab2ex3,Mettl3null/+ mutant females show approximately 3-fold higher viability (Figure 5A), 6-fold higher climbing rates (at the 30 s time point; Figure 5B), and 1.75-fold longer lifespan (Figure 5C) than Nab2ex3 mutant females.
evidence: This claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Nab2ex3,Mettl3null/+ mutant females show 6-fold higher climbing rates (at the 30 s time point) than Nab2ex3 mutant females.
source: However, Mettl3null heterozygosity has the inverse effect of suppressing each of these defects in Nab2ex3 females: Nab2ex3,Mettl3null/+ mutant females show approximately 3-fold higher viability (Figure 5A), 6-fold higher climbing rates (at the 30 s time point; Figure 5B), and 1.75-fold longer lifespan (Figure 5C) than Nab2ex3 mutant females.
evidence: This claim is supported by locomotion data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Nab2ex3,Mettl3null/+ mutant females show 1.75-fold longer lifespan than Nab2ex3 mutant females.
source: However, Mettl3null heterozygosity has the inverse effect of suppressing each of these defects in Nab2ex3 females: Nab2ex3,Mettl3null/+ mutant females show approximately 3-fold higher viability (Figure 5A), 6-fold higher climbing rates (at the 30 s time point; Figure 5B), and 1.75-fold longer lifespan (Figure 5C) than Nab2ex3 mutant females.
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Depletion of Mettl3 only in neurons is sufficient to suppress Nab2ex3-associated defects in viability in female flies.
source: Notably, this depletion of Mettl3 only in neurons was sufficient to suppress Nab2ex3-associated defects in both viability (Figure 5D) and locomotion (Figure 5E) in female flies, consistent with a functional interaction between Nab2 and Mettl3 in neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by neuron-specific RNAi data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Depletion of Mettl3 only in neurons is sufficient to suppress Nab2ex3-associated defects in locomotion in female flies.
source: Notably, this depletion of Mettl3 only in neurons was sufficient to suppress Nab2ex3-associated defects in both viability (Figure 5D) and locomotion (Figure 5E) in female flies, consistent with a functional interaction between Nab2 and Mettl3 in neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by neuron-specific RNAi data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Heterozygous loss of fl(2)d in a Nab2ex3 mutant suppresses defects in female locomotion but not viability.
source: Heterozygous loss of fl(2)d in a Nab2ex3 mutant suppresses defects in female locomotion but not viability, while heterozygous loss of virilizer dominantly suppresses defects in both viability and locomotion.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: Heterozygous loss of virilizer dominantly suppresses defects in both viability and locomotion in Nab2ex3 mutants.
source: Heterozygous loss of fl(2)d in a Nab2ex3 mutant suppresses defects in female locomotion but not viability, while heterozygous loss of virilizer dominantly suppresses defects in both viability and locomotion.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: MeRIP-qPCR detects reduced Sxl m6A in Mettl3null heads relative to controls.
source: This approach detects reduced Sxl m6A in Mettl3null heads relative to controls, which is consistent with prior studies (Haussmann et al., 2016; Lence et al., 2016; Kan et al., 2017; Kan et al., 2021), and an increase in Sxl transcript recovered from MeRIP of Nab2ex3 heads, consistent with increased Sxl m6A modification.
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP-qPCR data and citations to prior studies.

claim: MeRIP-qPCR detects an increase in Sxl transcript recovered from MeRIP of Nab2ex3 heads, consistent with increased Sxl m6A modification.
source: This approach detects reduced Sxl m6A in Mettl3null heads relative to controls, which is consistent with prior studies (Haussmann et al., 2016; Lence et al., 2016; Kan et al., 2017; Kan et al., 2021), and an increase in Sxl transcript recovered from MeRIP of Nab2ex3 heads, consistent with increased Sxl m6A modification.
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Act5c and Usp16 show decreased m6A in Mettl3null flies.
source: MeRIP-qPCR indicates that both mRNAs show decreased m6A in Mettl3null and show increased m6A in Nab2ex3 flies (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Act5c and Usp16 show increased m6A in Nab2ex3 flies.
source: MeRIP-qPCR indicates that both mRNAs show decreased m6A in Mettl3null and show increased m6A in Nab2ex3 flies (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: MeRIP analysis reveals moderate (1.5-fold) enrichment for intron 2-containing Sxl RNAs in Nab2ex3 heads.
source: MeRIP analysis using the I2-E3 primer pair (SxlI2-E3 in Figure 6C) or the I3-E4 primer pair (SxlI3-E4 in Figure 6C) reveals moderate (1.5-fold) enrichment for intron 2-containing Sxl RNAs in Nab2ex3 heads, and stronger (4.5-fold) enrichment for intron 3-containing RNAs, consistent with elevated m6A on Sxl pre-mRNAs that contain introns 2 and 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: MeRIP analysis reveals stronger (4.5-fold) enrichment for intron 3-containing Sxl RNAs in Nab2ex3 heads.
source: MeRIP analysis using the I2-E3 primer pair (SxlI2-E3 in Figure 6C) or the I3-E4 primer pair (SxlI3-E4 in Figure 6C) reveals moderate (1.5-fold) enrichment for intron 2-containing Sxl RNAs in Nab2ex3 heads, and stronger (4.5-fold) enrichment for intron 3-containing RNAs, consistent with elevated m6A on Sxl pre-mRNAs that contain introns 2 and 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: DART-Sanger sequencing revealed the presence of seven m6A sites within the Sxl exon 3-intron 3503 region.
source: Sanger sequencing and subsequent analysis of C-to-U transitions revealed the presence of seven m6A sites (sites #1–7) within this region (Figure 6D–F, denoted by asterisk in Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by DART-Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Four m6A sites show a statistically significant increase in C-to-U transition in Nab2ex3 female heads compared to control.
source: Of the seven m6A modifications mapped within this region, four sites show a statistically significant increases C-to-U transition in Nab2ex3 female heads compared to control (Figure 6D; four sites are denoted by red color in Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by DART-Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Sites 1–3 and 7 show 2.00 ratio of m6A modification (calculated as %C-to-U Nab2ex3/%C-to-U control).
source: Specifically, sites 1–3 and 7 show 2.00 ratio of m6A modification (calculated as %C-to-U Nab2ex3/%C-to-U control), providing evidence that these sites are methylated to a greater extent in Nab2ex3 female heads compared to control heads.
evidence: This claim is supported by DART-Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The m6A modification mapped to site 7 falls within the first adenosine residue of the proposed Nab2 AC(A)13 binding site.
source: Notably, the m6A modification mapped to site 7 falls within the first adenosine residue of the proposed Nab2 AC(A)13 binding site (see schematic in Figure 6A and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by DART-Sanger sequencing data and schematic shown in Figure 6A and F.

claim: Anti-Flag IP of FLAG-Nab2 provides evidence that Nab2 associates with unspliced Sxl pre-mRNA.
source: To test whether Nab2 physically associates with Sxl pre-mRNA as a potential mechanism to limit m6A levels, an anti-Flag IP of FLAG-Nab2 was performed from head lysates of adult females expressing N-terminally tagged Nab2 specifically in neurons (elav>Flag:Nab2). RT-qPCR of precipitates analyzed with Sxl I3-E4 primers provides evidence that Nab2 associates with unspliced Sxl pre-mRNA (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-IP data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Overexpression of Mettl3 in neurons is sufficient to produce the exon 3-exon 4 and exon 3-intron 3503-exon 4 RNAs in both control and Nab2ex3 heterozygote heads.
source: However, overexpression of Mettl3 in neurons is sufficient to produce the exon 3-exon 4 and exon 3-intron 3503-exon 4 RNAs in both control and Nab2ex3 heterozygote heads, thus replicating the effect of Nab2 loss on Sxl splicing.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Heterozygous loss of Ythdc1 increases viability of Nab2ex3 females approximately fivefold.
source: Indeed, heterozygous loss of Ythdc1 increases viability of Nab2ex3 females approximately fivefold (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Nab2 loss significantly alters splicing patterns within a small number of approximately 150 transcripts in female and male heads.
source: Through an unbiased high-throughput RNA sequencing approach, we identify a set of head-enriched RNAs in Drosophila whose levels or structure are significantly affected by loss of the Nab2 RBP, with the latter effect on RNA structure traced to splicing defects (including intron retention, alternative 5′ and 3′ splice site usage, and exon skipping) in a small group of approximately 150 transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and MISO/DEXSeq analysis.

claim: Nab2-Mettl3 coregulation of Sxl splicing is most significant in neurons.
source: Data suggest that Nab2-Mettl3 coregulation of Sxl splicing is most significant in neurons – the effect of Nab2 on Sxl splicing is strongest in tissues that contain CNS components (e.g., brain and ventral nerve cord), while Mettl3 overexpression only in neurons is sufficient to replicate Sxl splicing defects seen in Nab2 mutant heads.
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue-specific RT-PCR and neuron-specific overexpression data.

claim: Lethality of animals lacking both Nab2 and Mettl3 is consistent with only partial overlap between RNA targets of these two RBPs.
source: This apparent tissue specificity of the link between Nab2 and Mettl3 may help explain neurological defects in mice and humans lacking the Nab2 ortholog ZC13H14, although lethality of animals lacking both Nab2 and Mettl3 is consistent with only partial overlap between RNA targets of these two RBPs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from genetic data showing lethality of double mutants.

claim: Sxl exon 3 contains a translational termination (stop) codon.
source: Because Sxl exon 3 contains a translational termination (stop) codon, inclusion of this exon disrupts female-specific expression of Sxl protein, a U-rich RNA binding protein that controls somatic and germline sexual identity via effects on splicing and translation of target mRNAs (rev. in Penalva and Sánchez, 2003; Moschall et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and established knowledge.

claim: Inclusion of Sxl exon 3 disrupts female-specific expression of Sxl protein.
source: Because Sxl exon 3 contains a translational termination (stop) codon, inclusion of this exon disrupts female-specific expression of Sxl protein, a U-rich RNA binding protein that controls somatic and germline sexual identity via effects on splicing and translation of target mRNAs (rev. in Penalva and Sánchez, 2003; Moschall et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and established knowledge.

claim: Mis-spliced RNAs in Nab2 mutant female heads are enriched for bioinformatically predicted Sxl binding motifs.
source: Multiple lines of evidence suggest that Sxl mRNA may be a particularly significant target of Nab2 in neurons: mis-spliced RNAs in Nab2 mutant female heads are enriched for bioinformatically predicted Sxl binding motifs, and the SxlM8 allele that constitutively skips exon 3 (Barbash and Cline, 1995) substantially reverses developmental and behavioral defects in Nab2 null females (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by RBP motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The SxlM8 allele substantially reverses developmental and behavioral defects in Nab2 null females.
source: Multiple lines of evidence suggest that Sxl mRNA may be a particularly significant target of Nab2 in neurons: mis-spliced RNAs in Nab2 mutant female heads are enriched for bioinformatically predicted Sxl binding motifs, and the SxlM8 allele that constitutively skips exon 3 (Barbash and Cline, 1995) substantially reverses developmental and behavioral defects in Nab2 null females (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Alleles of male-specific DCC components rescue phenotypic defects in Nab2 mutant females.
source: Moving downstream of Sxl, alleles of male-specific DCC components, including the direct Sxl target msl-2 (Bashaw and Baker, 1995; Bashaw and Baker, 1997), also rescue phenotypic defects in Nab2 mutant females (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Masculinized Sxl splicing and DCC activity contribute to developmental and behavioral defects in Nab2 mutant female flies.
source: Given that these DCC components are not normally expressed or active in females, these data provide evidence that masculinized Sxl splicing and DCC activity contribute to developmental and behavioral defects in Nab2 mutant female flies.
evidence: This claim is inferred from genetic rescue data.

claim: Nab2 interacts with the Sxl pre-mRNA in the nucleus and opposes m6A methylation by the Mettl3 complex.
source: Given the known role of m6A in promoting Sxl exon 3 excision (Haussmann et al., 2016; Lence et al., 2016; Kan et al., 2017), these data collectively support a model in which Nab2 interacts with the Sxl pre-mRNA in the nucleus and opposes m6A methylation by the Mettl3 complex, thus ensuring a level of m6A necessary to guide Sxl exon 3 skipping in the female nervous system.
evidence: This claim is inferred from biochemical and genetic data.

claim: Either too little or too much m6A methylation of the region surrounding Sxl exon 3 can result in its retention in the developing female brain.
source: We term this a 'goldilocks' model in which either too little or too much m6A methylation of the region surrounding Sxl exon 3 can result in its retention in the developing female brain.
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain the data.

claim: Nab2 is required to limit m6A modification of an RNA.
source: These data provide the first evidence that the highly conserved Nab2 RBP is a key regulator of splicing in the adult brain, and that Nab2 is required to limit m6A modification of an RNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by MeRIP and DART data showing increased m6A in Nab2 mutants.

claim: Some fraction of the mis-spliced mRNAs detected by Nab2ex3 high-throughput sequencing may be Sxl targets.
source: Studies employing the SxlM8 allele indicate that altered Sxl splicing and decreased Sxl protein contribute to Nab2 mutant phenotypes in females. As Sxl is itself an RBP that can control splicing, some fraction of the mis-sliced mRNAs detected by Nab2ex3 high-throughput sequencing may thus be Sxl targets.
evidence: This claim is inferred from genetic rescue data and RBP motif enrichment.

claim: Splicing of the Sxl target RNA tra is unaffected in the Nab2 mutant RNA-Seq datasets.
source: However, splicing of the Sxl target RNA tra is unaffected in the Nab2 mutant RNA-Seq datasets.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A large majority of other mis-splicing events in Nab2 mutant head RNAs occur in both males and females.
source: Although this study focuses on Sxl as a female-specific Nab2 regulated RNA, a large majority of other mis-splicing events in Nab2 mutant head RNAs occur in both males and females.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and MISO/DEXSeq analysis.

claim: Approximately 100 intron-containing pre-mRNAs accumulate in nab2 mutant S. cerevisiae cells.
source: This evidence of a Nab2 role in non-sex-specific splicing events parallels evidence of accumulation of ~100 intron-containing pre-mRNAs in nab2 mutant S. cerevisiae cells (Soucek et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Soucek et al., 2016.

claim: Rescue of Nab2 mutant males and females by neuron-restricted expression of human ZC3H14 implies that this specificity may be conserved in ZC3H14 proteins in higher eukaryotes.
source: Rescue of Nab2 mutant males and females by neuron-restricted expression of human ZC3H14 (Kelly et al., 2014) implies that this specificity may be a conserved in ZC3H14 proteins in higher eukaryotes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from rescue data and citation to Kelly et al., 2014.

claim: Knockdown of ZC3H14 in cultured vertebrate cells results in pre-mRNA processing defects and intron-specific splicing defects.
source: Indeed, knockdown of ZC3H14 in cultured vertebrate cells results in pre-mRNA processing defects and intron-specific splicing defects in the few RNAs that have been examined (Morris and Corbett, 2018; Wigington et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morris and Corbett, 2018 and Wigington et al., 2016.

claim: Nab2 and ZC3H14 each co-purify at nearly stoichiometric levels with the exon junction complex (EJC).
source: However, recent studies demonstrating that Nab2 and ZC3H14 each co-purify at nearly stoichiometric levels with the exon junction complex (EJC) (Obrdlik et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2012) and that the EJC binding locally excludes Mettl3-mediated m6A deposition on pre-mRNAs (He et al., 2023; Uzonyi et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2022) suggest an alternate model in which Nab2 inhibits m6A deposition in cooperation with the EJC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Obrdlik et al., 2019 and Singh et al., 2012.

claim: The EJC binding locally excludes Mettl3-mediated m6A deposition on pre-mRNAs.
source: However, recent studies demonstrating that Nab2 and ZC3H14 each co-purify at nearly stoichiometric levels with the exon junction complex (EJC) (Obrdlik et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2012) and that the EJC binding locally excludes Mettl3-mediated m6A deposition on pre-mRNAs (He et al., 2023; Uzonyi et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2022) suggest an alternate model in which Nab2 inhibits m6A deposition in cooperation with the EJC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to He et al., 2023; Uzonyi et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2022.

claim: The human homolog of the Drosophila protein Virilizer was recovered in an IP/mass-spectrometry screen for ZC3H14 nuclear interactors.
source: Notably, the human homolog of the Drosophila protein Virilizer, which is an m6A methyltransferase subunit and splicing factor (Hilfiker et al., 1995; Niessen et al., 2001), was recovered in an IP/mass-spectrometry screen for ZC3H14 nuclear interactors (Morris and Corbett, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Morris and Corbett, 2018.

claim: Changes in abundance or structure of the group of Nab2-regulated RNAs may be due in part to changes in m6A status.
source: Moreover, evidence that m6A modulatory role of Nab2 is not restricted to the Sxl mRNA (see Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2) raises the additional hypothesis that changes in abundance or structure of the group of Nab2-regulated RNAs defined in this study (see Figures 1 and 2) are due in part to changes in m6A status.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on m6A data for Act5c and Usp16.

claim: Almost all developmental and behavioral defects caused by Nab2 loss can be traced to a Nab2 role within central nervous system neurons.
source: Prior work has shown that almost all developmental and behavioral defects caused by Nab2 loss can be traced to a Nab2 role within central nervous system neurons (Pak et al., 2011; Kelly et al., 2014; Kelly et al., 2016; Corgiat et al., 2022; Rounds et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Wwox RNA has a 3′UTR intron that is retained in Nab2 mutant heads.
source: Significantly, the Wwox RNA has a 3′UTR intron that is retained in Nab2 mutant heads (this study) and contains a candidate m6A site (Kan et al., 2021), suggesting that Wwox RNA may be a target of both Nab2 and Mettl3.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data from this study and citation to Kan et al., 2021.

claim: Elevated Wwox protein is detected in the hippocampus of ZC3H14 knockout mice.
source: Elevated Wwox protein is also detected in the hippocampus of ZC3H14 knockout mice, raising the possibility that Nab2 and ZC3H14 share some common RNA targets across species (Roxas et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Roxas et al., 2017.

claim: ZC3H14 has to date not been linked to the m6A mark in mouse or human cells.
source: ZC3H14 has to date not been linked to the m6A mark in mouse or human cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The Nab2/ZC3H14 family of RBPs may share an m6A inhibitory role that is specific to neurons.
source: However, the enrichment for Sxl mis-splicing in neuronal tissue (see Figure 3F) and rescue by ZC3H14 when expressed in neurons of otherwise Nab2-deficient animals (Kelly et al., 2016) supports the hypothesis that the Nab2/ZC3H14 family of RBPs may share an m6A inhibitory role that is specific to neurons, and that excessive m6A methylation of RNAs also contributes to neurological deficits in mice and humans lacking ZC3H14.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on tissue-specific data and rescue experiments.

claim: Excessive m6A methylation of RNAs may contribute to neurological deficits in mice and humans lacking ZC3H14.
source: However, the enrichment for Sxl mis-splicing in neuronal tissue (see Figure 3F) and rescue by ZC3H14 when expressed in neurons of otherwise Nab2-deficient animals (Kelly et al., 2016) supports the hypothesis that the Nab2/ZC3H14 family of RBPs may share an m6A inhibitory role that is specific to neurons, and that excessive m6A methylation of RNAs also contributes to neurological deficits in mice and humans lacking ZC3H14.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on data from Drosophila.
